extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent attorneys, and applicants working with Korean patent law / KIPO
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining novelty under the Korean Patent Act (Article 29), including what constitutes prior art (publicly known/practiced, distributed publications, telecommunication disclosures), how to interpret claim language, and evidentiary/credibility rules for internet disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for Patentability (Article 29)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention having industrial applicability, other than the following, is patentable: (1) An invention publicly known or practiced within or outside of the Republic of Korea prior to filing; (2) An invention published in a publication distributed within or outside of the Republic of Korea or an invention made available to the public via telecommunications lines prior to filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purport: The patent system grants an exclusive right as a reward for disclosure; inventions already disclosed to the public shall not be given exclusive rights. Under Article 29(1), prior-to-filing disclosures by public knowledge, public practice, publications, or telecommunication availability mean lack of novelty and non-patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'Publicly Known Invention'
rubrics_metrics.description: 『A publicly known invention』means an invention the contents of which have been known to an unspecified person without obligation of secrecy in the Republic of Korea or a foreign country prior to the filing of the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing time is the exact point (hour and minute); 'unspecified persons' = general public not bound by secrecy. Example: an application not laid open and not published after registration is not prior art under distributed publication rule but may become prior art upon public inspection after registration (Article 20).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'Publicly Practiced Invention'
rubrics_metrics.description: 『A publicly practiced invention』means an invention which has been practiced under conditions where the contents of the invention are to be publicly known or can potentially be publicly known in the Republic of Korea or a foreign country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 『Being public』means no longer kept secret. If only a small part of technical features is secret with regard to practicing, it shall not be considered publicly practiced. Examples: observing a manufacturing process at a plant exposed to unspecified persons; or situations where inner parts are not visible but visitors may inspect or be explained those inner parts (i.e., refusal to allow observation/explanation matters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'Distributed Publication'
rubrics_metrics.description: A publication is 'a document, a drawing or other similar medium ... duplicated by printing, mechanical or chemical methods, etc. for the purpose of disclosing the contents to the public through distribution'. 'Distribution' means placing such a publication where unspecified persons can read or see it; actual access is not required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent gazettes on microfilm or CD‑ROM, non‑patent documents stored on floppy discs/slides/presentations/microfilm/CD‑ROM are considered distributed publications if produced to make available to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time of Distribution (dated publications)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the time of publication is indicated in a publication, it is presumed as follows: (a) only year → last day of year; (b) month and year → last day of that month; (c) day, month, year → that date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where no date is indicated: (a) foreign publications' distribution date is presumed based on normal transit time to Korea if receipt in Korea is clear; (b) derivative publications use the derivative's publication date; (c) second editions/publishes presume first edition date if contents accord; (d) other appropriate information may be used to presume/estimate date.

rubrics_metrics.name: What it Means to be 'Described in a Publication'
rubrics_metrics.description: 『An invention described in a publication』means an invention identified by the matters described or essentially described, though not literally, in a publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Matters essentially described' are those directly derivable from matters described, considering common general knowledge. Example: a utility innovation must have at least its configuration described — mere photographs of an internal technical feature may not suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventions Made Available via Telecommunication Lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Telecommunication line disclosures (including internet, public bulletin boards, e‑mail groups) can be prior art if the invention is made available to the public through those lines; telecommunication includes transmission/reception by wired, wireless, optic, or other electromagnetic processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CD‑ROMs or diskettes are not telecommunication disclosures but are treated as distributed publications. The definition extends to future electronic/telecommunication methods as technology advances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of Patent Act Revision on Telecommunication Disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Before the 2013 revision, inventions made available via telecommunication lines designated by Presidential Decree had the same status as published inventions. The 2013 revision deleted the phrase 'designated by Presidential Decree' so inventions made available over all telecommunication lines fall under Article 29(1)(ii) for applications filed after July 1, 2013.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus citation rules differ by application filing date: (i) applications filed before June 30, 2013 may be cited under the prior law depending on whether the telecommunication line was designated; (ii) applications filed after July 1, 2013 are cited under the revised Article 29(1)(ii).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for 'Available to the Public' for Telecommunication Disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: To cite an invention disclosed through telecommunication lines as prior art described in publications, the invention shall be 'the one available to the public'. 'Available to the public' means the invention can be seen by an unspecified person and does not require actual access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If disclosure is only accessible by a specific person or is restricted, it is not considered available. For websites, determining availability includes whether the site is findable by a general search engine or encoded so it cannot generally be read. Only information considered available to the public can be cited as prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Telecommunication Lines Deemed Reliable (pre‑revision Article 1‑2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Telecommunication lines operated by the following are treated as having credibility: (i) governments/local governments/foreign governments/international organizations; (ii) national/public schools or foreign national/public universities; (iii) national/public research institutes (domestic or foreign); (iv) corporations designated and publicly notified by the Commissioner of KIPO (e.g., KIPA, Korea Institute of Patent Information).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosures on these lines may be cited as prior art without additional confirmation. 'International organization' means intergovernmental organizations (e.g., UN, WIPO, WTO, EPO) but not NGOs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of Disclosure Content and Time (evidence standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: To cite prior art for novelty/inventive step, the examiner shall present evidence that the prior art was disclosed at the indicated time; this applies equally to telecommunication disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For: (i) designated or sufficiently credible telecommunication lines, examiner may accept disclosure content/time without extra confirmation; (ii) other lines, examiner must assess credibility based on public awareness, use frequency, operator credibility, operation period, etc.; (iii) where credibility is in doubt, the examiner must confirm actual disclosure date (e.g., contact person in charge or use Internet Archive archive.org). The disclosure time is the instant the invention was disclosed on the telecommunication line (even if same content appeared earlier in a distributed publication).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Citation for Electronic Technical Information
rubrics_metrics.description: When citing electronic technical information retrieved from telecommunication lines, bibliographical items (author, title, publication name, pages/drawings/graph) shall be listed in order in compliance with WIPO Standards ST.14.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a cited document is a patent published through the Internet, the examiner may describe it in the same way as patent official gazettes (CD‑ROM form) without needing the date of searching and website address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of Hyperlinked Other Websites
rubrics_metrics.description: Websites hyperlinked from reliable telecommunication lines are not themselves considered to be the same reliable telecommunication lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hyperlinked sites' credibility regarding disclosure time cannot be guaranteed because they are run by other entities; therefore hyperlinks do not confer the same reliability for citation purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination When Applicant Opposes Telecommunication Disclosure Citation
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant raises opposition/evidence questioning accessibility, disclosure content, or disclosure time of a telecommunication line disclosure, the examiner shall consider such grounds/evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If credibility becomes doubtful, the examiner must search additional evidence to confirm the disclosure. If no additional evidence can be found, the invention disclosed on the telecommunication line cannot be cited as prior art. If the applicant only provides unsupported arguments (e.g., merely asserts unreliability without specifics), the examiner need not consider them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of Novelty (general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner shall determine novelty by judging whether the claimed invention falls under inventions categorized in Article 29(1) subparagraphs (1) to (2). If it falls under those categories, the invention is not novel; otherwise it is novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must describe the subject matter for which protection is sought (Article 42(4)). Identicalness of invention is determined by identicalness of matters described in the claims. Each claim is judged separately when there are multiple claims in an application.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Principle of Defining the Claimed Invention (claim language clear)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the claim language is clear, defining the claimed invention should be made as recited in the claim. Terminology in claims is interpreted with the general meaning and scope generally accepted in the technical field, except where a specific meaning is explicitly defined in the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation should be objective and reasonable considering ordinary skill at filing. Avoid limiting a clear claim by reference to description/drawings unless the claim itself requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding Undue Limitation by Description or Drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: Where claim description is clear, an examiner should avoid limited interpretation just by referencing the description of the invention or drawings. Matters not described in the claims but only in the description/drawings should be considered as not recited in the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An examiner should not examine claims by applying subject matters not described in the claims. Examples: (i) 'cream' in claims should not be limited to a specific embodiment in description; (ii) 'thin film type probe' claim should not be limited to a specific pattern shown in the embodiment; (iii) rotation direction shown in drawings does not limit claim if not claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's Specific Definition in Description
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant specifically defines a term in the description so that it is clearly different from the general meaning, the term is interpreted as having that specific meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, merely describing a specific embodiment or concept in the description and drawings does not automatically create a specific definition for the term. Terms are to be interpreted with their general technical meaning unless a clear, explicit definition is provided and intended to depart from the general meaning. Also, terms should be unified over the whole specification.
